artiest/big-joe-turner.text:
Big Joe Turner was an American blues shouter from Kansas City, Missouri, born on 18 May 1911. His father was killed in a train accident when Joe was four. He sang in church and on street corners, left school at fourteen and worked in the nightclubs of Kansas City, first as a cook and later as a singing bartender. That earned him the nickname The Singing Barman. Together with his friend, the pianist Pete Johnson, he performed in clubs such as the Sunset. In 1938 the talent scout John Hammond saw them and invited them to play at Carnegie Hall in the concert series From Spirituals to Swing.

Hits followed, such as Roll 'Em Pete, a collection of traditional blues lyrics that Turner often recorded again. From 1939 Turner and Johnson played with the boogie-woogie pianists Albert Ammons and Meade Lux Lewis at Café Society in New York, appearing alongside Billie Holiday, among others. Cherry Red and Wee Baby Blues date from that period too. In 1941 he appeared in Duke Ellington's revue Jump for Joy, and in 1945 he signed with National Records.

He achieved his greatest fame in the 1950s with rock 'n' roll recordings, above all Shake, Rattle and Roll. Even so, his career ran from the 1920s to the 1980s. In 1987 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame, which called him a voice with power. The songwriter Doc Pomus said that rock 'n' roll would never have come into being without him. Turner joined the blues and boogie-woogie of Kansas City to the young rock 'n' roll.
artiest/big-joe-turner.listen: Listen to Shake, Rattle and Roll and notice his voice: he does not shout, but sings with power and lets the band drive him on. Notice, too, how strong the backbeat is.

artiest/big-joe-turner-en-pete-johnson.text:
Joe Turner was born in Kansas City, Missouri, in 1911. He left school at fourteen to work in the city's nightclubs, first as a cook and later as a singing bartender, which gave him the nickname The Singing Barman. In clubs such as the Kingfish Club and the Sunset, his friend Pete Johnson played piano. The partnership was a fruitful one. In 1936 they tried their luck in New York, but the city was not yet ready for them. In 1938 the talent scout John Hammond saw them and brought them back for a concert in the series From Spirituals to Swing at Carnegie Hall, intended to bring jazz and blues to a broader American audience.

After that appearance they had a big success with Roll 'Em Pete from 1938, a collection of traditional blues lines set to a driving boogie-woogie rhythm. Turner would go on to record the song many times over the following years. In 1939, together with the boogie-woogie pianists Albert Ammons and Meade Lux Lewis, they began a residency at the New York club Café Society, where Billie Holiday also performed.

Turner was a blues shouter: a singer with a powerful voice who could carry above a band without a microphone. His greatest fame came in the 1950s with rock 'n' roll recordings such as Shake, Rattle and Roll, and in 1987 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. The songwriter Doc Pomus said that rock 'n' roll would never have come into being without him.
artiest/big-joe-turner-en-pete-johnson.listen: Listen to Roll 'Em Pete. Notice how Johnson's left hand plays a steady, rolling boogie-woogie bass, while Turner sings over it in a broad, powerful voice.

artiest/big-mama-thornton.text:
Willie Mae Thornton, known as Big Mama Thornton, was born in 1926 in Ariton, Alabama. She taught herself to sing, drum and play the harmonica, and from about the age of fourteen she toured with Sammy Green's Hot Harlem Revue. She is important because she was the first to record Hound Dog, years before Elvis Presley, and because her raw way of singing became the model for Janis Joplin.

In 1950 Thornton signed with Peacock Records, a label from Houston. In 1952 she joined Johnny Otis's rhythm and blues revue. That year the young songwriters Jerry Leiber and Mike Stoller wrote Hound Dog for her: a raw blues in which a woman shows a man the door. Otis played drums on the recording. In 1953 the song spent seven weeks at number 1 on the Billboard R&B chart, and according to the label boss Don Robey it sold between 500,000 and 750,000 copies. Thornton herself said that she received a single royalty cheque for it, for 500 dollars.

In 1956 Elvis Presley recorded Hound Dog, faster and with different words. His version is estimated to have sold about ten million copies. The money went to the writers and the publisher, not to the singer who had recorded it first. Thornton also wrote songs herself, including Ball and Chain. Janis Joplin made it famous with Big Brother and the Holding Company, at the Monterey Pop Festival of 1967 and on the album Cheap Thrills (1968). Thornton died in 1984 in Los Angeles. That same year she was inducted into the Blues Hall of Fame.
artiest/big-mama-thornton.listen: Hound Dog (1953): notice how Thornton growls and mocks the words more than she sings them, over a slow, dragging rhythm. Then compare the tempo with the fast version by Elvis Presley from 1956.

artiest/big-star.text:
Big Star was an American rock band from Memphis, Tennessee. The group formed in 1971 around Alex Chilton and Chris Bell, both singers and guitarists, with Andy Hummel on bass and Jody Stephens on drums. As a sixteen-year-old, Chilton had had a number 1 hit with The Letter, as the singer of the Box Tops. Big Star gained a reputation as a quintessential American power pop band, with influences from the Beatles and the Byrds of the 1960s.

The debut #1 Record from 1972 received enthusiastic reviews, but poor promotion and limited distribution by the label Stax meant few sales. Bell left, and the second album, Radio City, completed in December 1973 and featuring September Gurls, also suffered from problems at the label, now Columbia. A third album from the autumn of 1974 was first shelved, and the band fell apart at the end of that year. In 1978 the first two records were released together in the United Kingdom, followed by Third/Sister Lovers. Shortly afterwards Chris Bell died in a car accident, aged 27.

Big Star's influence grew after the break-up. Bands such as R.E.M. and the Replacements cited the group as an example, and the music pointed ahead to the alternative rock of the 1980s and 1990s. In 1993 Chilton and Stephens came together again with Jon Auer and Ken Stringfellow of the Posies, and in 2005 In Space was released. Chilton died in 2010, Hummel a few months later.
artiest/big-star.listen: Listen to September Gurls. Notice the bright, jangling guitars and the sweet melody beneath which a sad story hides.

artiest/big-youth.text:
Big Youth is the stage name of Manley Augustus Buchanan, a Jamaican deejay who had his greatest influence in the 1970s. He was born on 19 April 1949 in Trenchtown, Kingston. Before making music he worked as a diesel mechanic at the Sheraton Hotel in Kingston, where colleagues called him Big Youth and where he developed his toasting. He began at dances, at first under the influence of U-Roy, and around 1970 became the regular deejay of the sound system of Lord Tippertone. Of the deejays he said himself that they stood closest to the people, because there was no control by the establishment over the sound systems.

His first singles for Jimmy Radway, Lee Perry and Phil Pratt did not catch on. He then worked with the young producer Gussie Clarke, and The Killer became his first big hit in Jamaica, followed by Tippertone Rocking. S-90 Skank, with a screaming engine in the studio, became his first number one. His first album was Chi Chi Run in 1972, followed by Screaming Target, a classic of the genre, and by Dreadlocks Dread in 1976. In 1973 he showed his dreadlocks during a performance, at a time when Rastafari musicians were often sidelined in the Jamaican music world. Later he released self-produced records.

Big Youth stood out for a half-sung style, unlike his colleagues, and for his teeth, which were inlaid with red, gold and green gemstones. He is one of the deejays who brought toasting from the dance floor to the record, and his style showed how Rastafari and street life could come together in the reggae song.
artiest/big-youth.listen: Listen to S-90 Skank and notice the sound of the engine in the recording. Hear how he moves back and forth between talking and singing over a relaxed reggae rhythm.

artiest/bikini-kill.text:
Bikini Kill is an American punk band from Olympia, in the state of Washington, formed in October 1990. The singer and lyricist Kathleen Hanna, the bassist Kathi Wilcox and the drummer Tobi Vail knew each other from The Evergreen State College. The guitarist Billy Karren completed the band. Hanna also made a fanzine called Bikini Kill. The band became the vanguard of riot grrrl, a feminist movement within punk.

Bikini Kill's music is raw, fast and abrasive, with influences from hardcore: short songs, hard guitars, rattling drums and Hanna's screaming, sharp voice. The lyrics dealt with sexism, violence against women and power. At concerts the band asked women to come to the front and handed out lyrics. Hanna sometimes jumped into the crowd herself to remove men who were heckling her. After a first demo, an EP appeared on the label Kill Rock Stars, produced by Ian MacKaye of Fugazi. The debut album Pussy Whipped came out in 1993. Joan Jett, who saw Hanna as an early example of riot grrrl, produced the single Rebel Girl.

The media attention for riot grrrl became so great that the band asked for a media blackout, because they felt they were being misrepresented. At concerts the band also met with a great deal of hostility. After Reject All American (1996), Bikini Kill broke up in 1997. Hanna went on to start Le Tigre. Since 2019 the band has been performing again. Bikini Kill showed that punk, which considered itself rebellious, was also a man's world.
artiest/bikini-kill.listen: Listen to Rebel Girl from 1993. Notice the stomping drums and the simple, hard guitar riff, and how Kathleen Hanna shouts the words rather than sings them.

artiest/bilal.text:
Bilal Sayeed Oliver, known as Bilal, is an American singer and songwriter, born on 23 August 1979 in Germantown, Philadelphia. His mother was Christian and his father Muslim. At eleven he became choir director at his mother's church, and at fourteen he founded a group that performed in Philadelphia. His father took him to jazz clubs, where he decided he wanted to be in music. He studied at The New School for Jazz and Contemporary Music in New York, where on his first day he met the pianist Robert Glasper. Through the New York clubs he came into contact with the Soulquarians, the collective of The Roots, Common, Erykah Badu and Mos Def, among others.

The demo he recorded with Aaron Comess of the Spin Doctors won him a contract with Interscope. He made his debut in 2000 with the R&B single Soul Sista and in 2001 released the album 1st Born Second, with contributions from the Soulquarians and from producers such as Dr. Dre and J Dilla. His second album, Love for Sale, leaked without ever being officially released, but received great praise. Later came Airtight's Revenge in 2010, A Love Surreal in 2013 and In Another Life in 2015, now as an independent artist. In 2020, during lockdown, he recorded the EP Voyage-19 in three days with musicians working remotely.

Bilal is known for his wide vocal range, his work across several genres and his intense live performances. He showed how soul, jazz and experimental music can flow into one another. He has collaborated with Kendrick Lamar, Common, Erykah Badu, Jay-Z, Beyoncé and The Roots, among others.
artiest/bilal.listen: Listen to Soul Sista from 2000 and notice his voice, which glides smoothly from low to high. Try to hear whether he sings more like an R&B star or like a jazz singer.

artiest/bill-black.text:
Bill Black was an American bassist and bandleader, born on 17 September 1926 in Memphis, Tennessee, the eldest of nine children. His father played banjo and fiddle for the family. At fourteen Bill learned to play on a homemade instrument made from a cigar box with a plank and strings, and at sixteen he was playing honky-tonk on acoustic guitar in bars. After his military service he married in 1946 and worked in a factory in Memphis. He switched to the upright double bass, with a slapping technique modelled on Fred Maddox, and on stage he liked to play the clown: an exaggerated hillbilly with blacked-out teeth, a straw hat and dungarees.

In 1952 he played with the guitarist Scotty Moore in clubs and on the radio, including in the band of Doug Poindexter. In July 1954 Sam Phillips of Sun Records asked them to accompany a still unknown singer, Elvis Presley. On 5 July 1954 they recorded songs at the Sun studios, and during a break Presley began to play around with That's All Right (Mama) by Arthur Crudup. Black and Moore joined in and Phillips set the tape rolling. The next day came Blue Moon of Kentucky, by Bill Monroe, which according to the sources Black kicked off, and which was then recorded in a fast version. That trio was called the Blue Moon Boys.

Later Black founded Bill Black's Combo. He is among the first rock 'n' roll musicians, and his slap bass gave Presley's early recordings their rhythm and their sharp, bouncing character. Black died on 21 October 1965.
artiest/bill-black.listen: Listen to That's All Right (Mama) from 1954 and focus on the double bass. Hear how the bass keeps the beat with slaps, without drums.

artiest/bill-dixon.text:
Bill Dixon was an American trumpeter, composer and teacher, born on 5 October 1925 in Nantucket, Massachusetts. In 1934 his family moved to Harlem in New York. He entered the army in 1944, served in Germany and afterwards studied music at the Hartnette Conservatory of Music with support from the GI Bill. He also studied painting. From 1956 to 1962 he worked at the United Nations, where he founded the UN Jazz Society.

In the 1960s he became a leading figure of the jazz avant-garde. In 1964 he organised the October Revolution in Jazz, four days of music and discussion at the Cellar Café in Manhattan, with Cecil Taylor and Sun Ra, among others. It was the first festival for free jazz. He co-founded the Jazz Composers Guild, which was meant to give musicians more bargaining power against club owners. He also worked with the dancer Judith Dunn, for whom he combined music and improvised dance. In 1967 RCA Victor released his first album under his own name, Intents and Purposes. From 1968 to 1995 he taught at Bennington College in Vermont, where he set up a department of Black music.

Dixon played trumpet, flugelhorn and piano, often with electronic echo and reverb. He used the low pedal register, far below the normal range of the trumpet, and also played without the usual attack. Later he worked with Cecil Taylor, Tony Oxley, William Parker and Rob Mazurek. He was regarded as one of the founders of free jazz and died on 16 June 2010.
artiest/bill-dixon.listen: Listen to a piece from the 1964 album Bill Dixon 7-Tette and notice the trumpet. Try to hear whether he plays with a clear tone or rather with low, rough and muted sounds.

artiest/bill-evans.text: The pianist Bill Evans, from New Jersey, studied classical music and played both Bud Powell and the French composers Debussy and Ravel. In 1958 he spent eight months with Miles Davis; his calm, open chords shaped the sound of Kind of Blue. He co-wrote Blue in Green. With the bassist Scott LaFaro and the drummer Paul Motian he formed a trio in 1959 in which the three players converse as equals. In June 1961 the trio recorded Sunday at the Village Vanguard and Waltz for Debby at the Village Vanguard; eleven days later LaFaro was killed in a car accident. Evans's way of playing chords, without the root note, became standard in jazz piano.
artiest/bill-evans.listen: Listen to how bass and piano play melodies at the same time, as if they were talking to each other.

artiest/bill-haley.text:
Bill Haley was born on 6 July 1925 in Highland Park, Michigan, and grew up in Pennsylvania. His father played banjo and mandolin, and his mother was a classically trained keyboard player. Because of an operation in childhood he was blind in one eye. The curl on his forehead was supposed to hide that side, but became his trademark.

Haley began in country music. In 1947 he founded a western swing band that later came to be called The Saddlemen, and in 1951 they recorded a cover of Rocket 88. In 1952 the name became Bill Haley with Haley's Comets, after Halley's Comet. Crazy Man, Crazy became a hit in 1953 and is sometimes called the first rock 'n' roll record. In 1954 he recorded Rock Around the Clock. The record did little at first, but after the song was heard in the film Blackboard Jungle, it reached number 1 in July 1955. Shake, Rattle and Roll and See You Later, Alligator also became big hits.

Haley mixed country music and western swing with Black rhythm and blues into a rousing new sound. Many regard him as the one who first made rock 'n' roll popular in the early 1950s, and his performances in Europe caused an uproar. Even so, his star was quick to fall: next to younger and wilder stars such as Elvis Presley, he looked like a man in his thirties with no sex appeal. He died on 9 February 1981 and was posthumously inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987.
artiest/bill-haley.listen: Listen to Shake, Rattle and Roll (1954). Haley took a slow blues by Big Joe Turner, sped it up and added the swing of country music. Notice how the saxophone and the slap bass make the song dance.

artiest/bill-haley-en-his-comets.text:
Bill Haley & His Comets came from Chester, Pennsylvania. The singer and guitarist Bill Haley started a western swing group in 1947, which later became known as Bill Haley and the Saddlemen. In 1952 it became Bill Haley & His Comets, and the music shifted towards rhythm and blues. The group is important because Rock Around the Clock was the first rock 'n' roll recording to top the American Billboard pop chart.

Crazy Man, Crazy (1953), on the small label Essex, was their first national success. The group then moved to Decca, where Milt Gabler produced all their records. On 12 April 1954 they recorded Rock Around the Clock in New York. It is a 12-bar blues, played on double bass, steel guitar, piano and tenor saxophone, among other instruments. Danny Cedrone played the fast guitar solo. Shake, Rattle and Roll, a cover of Big Joe Turner, became Haley's first gold record later that year. Rock Around the Clock only really took off when it was heard under the opening credits of the film Blackboard Jungle in 1955. On 9 July 1955 it reached number 1, where it stayed for eight weeks.

In February 1957 the group came to England. At Waterloo station in London the musicians were overwhelmed by fans; the press spoke of the 'Second Battle of Waterloo'. The Guinness Book of Records estimated the sales of Haley's version at some 15 million copies, although that figure has never been verified. Haley died in 1981. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987, the Comets in 2012.
artiest/bill-haley-en-his-comets.listen: Rock Around the Clock (1954): count the bars in a verse. There are twelve, with three chords: the pattern of the blues. Then notice the fast guitar solo by Danny Cedrone, which he had already played in 1952 on Rock the Joint.

artiest/bill-justis.text:
Bill Justis was an American saxophonist, trumpeter, arranger and producer, born on 14 October 1926 in Birmingham, Alabama. He grew up in Memphis and studied music at Christian Brothers College and at Tulane University in New Orleans, where he played with jazz and dance bands. In 1951 he returned to Memphis and joined Sam Phillips at Sun Records. There he recorded his own music and wrote arrangements for Sun artists such as Jerry Lee Lewis, Roy Orbison, Johnny Cash and Charlie Rich, whom according to the source he discovered.

His best-known piece is Raunchy, released in September 1957. He wrote it together with Sid Manker. It is the first rock 'n' roll instrumental to become a hit. It reached number two in the United States in three versions, alongside those of Ernie Freeman and Billy Vaughn, and later entered the Grammy Hall of Fame. A second hit was College Man. In 1961 he moved to Nashville, where he became a producer and arranger for pop and country artists at Monument and Mercury. He played saxophone on the soundtrack of the Elvis film Kissin' Cousins in 1964 and wrote music for films, including Smokey and the Bandit in 1977. In Australia he had a number one in 1963 with Tamoure.

Justis built the bridge between the early rock 'n' roll of Sun and the Nashville studios. With Raunchy he showed that a saxophone and a sharp guitar without a singer could make a hit. He died in 1982 in Nashville.
artiest/bill-justis.listen: Listen to Raunchy from 1957 and notice what plays the melody in place of a singing voice. Hear how saxophone and guitar take turns over a steady, stomping accompaniment.

artiest/bill-laswell.text:
Bill Laswell is an American bass guitarist, producer and label owner, born on 12 February 1955 in Salem, Illinois. His family moved often and eventually settled in Michigan, where the music scene in the 1960s and 1970s was broad, from Motown to Detroit's young punk and rock circuit. Laswell taught himself to play bass and looked for an unusual approach: he wanted to use the bass to create soundscapes, not merely to carry the rhythm. He played in R&B and funk bands and saw concerts by Iggy and the Stooges, MC5 and Funkadelic. He also listened to John Coltrane, Albert Ayler and Miles Davis.

In the late 1970s he moved to New York, where he joined the group that became the first version of Material. Material accompanied Daevid Allen and New York Gong. Laswell worked with Brian Eno, Fred Frith, John Zorn, Ginger Baker and Peter Brötzmann, and became house producer at Celluloid Records. There he recorded experimental music that mixed jazz, funk, pop and R&B, with Sonny Sharrock, Archie Shepp and Henry Threadgill, among others. He has been involved in thousands of recordings and made albums such as Baselines in 1983, Low Life in 1987 and Silent Recoil: Dub System One in 1995. His band Praxis often featured the guitarist Buckethead.

Laswell is known for his idea of collision music: bringing together musicians from very different worlds and seeing what comes out. His music draws on funk, world music, jazz, dub and ambient. In this way he is an important link between the New York avant-garde, dub and world music.
artiest/bill-laswell.listen: Listen to a piece from Silent Recoil: Dub System One from 1995 and focus on the bass. Notice how heavy and deep it sounds, and how the other sounds float around it like echoes.

artiest/bill-monroe.text:
Bill Monroe was born in 1911 on a farm near Rosine, Kentucky, the youngest of eight children. Because his older brothers already played fiddle and guitar, the mandolin was what was left for him. After the death of his parents he lived with his uncle Pen Vandiver, a fiddler who played at dances. Bill accompanied him and in this way learned the old fiddle tunes. From the Black musician Arnold Shultz he got to know the blues.

In the 1930s he played with his brother Charlie as the Monroe Brothers on radio and on records. In 1939 he founded the Blue Grass Boys in Atlanta, named after the bluegrass of Kentucky. That same year he won a regular spot on the Grand Ole Opry. When the guitarist Lester Flatt and the banjo player Earl Scruggs joined at the end of 1945, the sound was complete. Breakneck tempos, high harmony singing and virtuoso solos on mandolin, banjo and fiddle: that was what bluegrass sounded like. In 1946 and 1947 the band recorded classics, including Blue Moon of Kentucky.

Monroe described his music as a mixture of Scottish bagpipes, old-time fiddle music, church music, blues and jazz, with a high and lonesome sound. The genre took its name from his band, and he was called the father of bluegrass. In 1954 Elvis Presley recorded Blue Moon of Kentucky as a fast rock 'n' roll version, and Monroe gave it his blessing. In this way he stands at the roots of both country and rock 'n' roll.
artiest/bill-monroe.listen: Listen to Blue Moon of Kentucky by Bill Monroe and then to the version by Elvis Presley. With Monroe, notice the mandolin, the fiddle and the high, plaintive singing, and hear how Presley makes something quite different of the same song.

artiest/bill-monroe-en-his-blue-grass-bo.text:
Bill Monroe was born in 1911 on a farm near Rosine, in Kentucky, the youngest of eight children. His brothers already played fiddle and guitar, so the mandolin was what was left for him. After the death of his parents he grew up with relatives and accompanied his uncle Pen Vandiver, a fiddle player, at dances. That experience later gave rise to the song Uncle Pen. The fiddler and guitarist Arnold Shultz also played a part, as he introduced Monroe to the blues.

In 1929 Monroe moved to Indiana, where with his brothers Birch and Charlie he formed the Monroe Brothers. The duo performed on the radio and in 1936 signed with RCA Victor. After they split up in 1938, Bill started his own group. He called it the Blue Grass Boys, after the bluegrass of his home state of Kentucky. The genre bluegrass got its name from that name. Blue Moon of Kentucky from 1947 belongs to this early period.

Monroe himself described bluegrass as Scottish bagpipes and old-time fiddling, with Methodists, Holiness and Baptists in it, and blues and jazz, with a high lonesome sound. It is acoustic music with fast mandolin, banjo, fiddle and guitar and high, searing singing. Because he created the genre, he is called the Father of Bluegrass. He died in 1996, four days before his 85th birthday.
artiest/bill-monroe-en-his-blue-grass-bo.listen: Listen to Blue Moon of Kentucky. Notice the high, piercing singing and Monroe's mandolin, which carries rhythm and melody at the same time.

artiest/bill-summers.text:
Bill Summers is an American percussionist who plays Afro-Cuban jazz and Latin jazz. He was born on 27 June 1948 and is a multi-instrumentalist, but plays mainly conga. His name is seldom out in front, because a large part of his work was done behind the scenes, in studios and on films. Even so, his career runs through several worlds: jazz, funk, Latin and film music.

In the 1970s he founded Bill Summers & Summers Heat, a large group with many musicians, including the saxophonist Hadley Caliman, the pianist Rodney Franklin and the guitarist Ray Obiedo. Between 1977 and 1983 the group made seven albums, with titles such as Cayenne, Straight to the Bank and Seventeen. Before that he played with Herbie Hancock in the days of The Headhunters. His contribution to the later album Evolution Revolution from 2003 is mentioned in the liner notes. He also worked on the music for films such as The Color Purple and on the television series Roots, together with Quincy Jones.

In the 1990s Summers played in Los Hombres Calientes, with the trumpeter Irvin Mayfield as co-leader and Jason Marsalis on drums. His solo work includes Feel the Heat from 1976 and The Essence of Kwanzaa from 1997. With his conga playing he showed how African and Cuban rhythms could gain a permanent place in American jazz and funk.
artiest/bill-summers.listen: Find a recording by Bill Summers & Summers Heat, for instance the album Cayenne, and listen only to the congas. Try to hear how they carry the rhythm alongside the bass and the horns.

artiest/bill-withers.text:
Bill Withers was born in 1938 in Slab Fork, a mining town in West Virginia, the youngest of six children. As a child he stuttered and felt like an outsider. At seventeen he joined the navy, where he stayed for nine years and began to sing and write songs. In 1967 he moved to Los Angeles. By day he worked in factories, including for aircraft manufacturers, and he recorded demos with his own money.

In 1970 he signed with Sussex Records. Booker T. Jones produced his debut Just As I Am (1971); on the cover Withers stands at his workplace with his lunch pail. Ain't No Sunshine became a hit and won a Grammy. Even so, he at first did not want to give up his job, because he did not trust the music world. Still Bill (1972) included Lean on Me, which reached number 1, and Use Me. Later, at Columbia, came Lovely Day (1977), among others, and, with the saxophonist Grover Washington Jr., Just the Two of Us (1980), which again won a Grammy.

Withers wrote simple, warm soul songs about ordinary people, love and friendship. His singing was understated and direct, without big flourishes. In the mid-1980s he largely stopped, tired of the hassle with record companies. His songs remained and are still widely covered. In 2015 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. He died in 2020.
artiest/bill-withers.listen: Listen to Just the Two of Us by Grover Washington Jr. with Bill Withers. Notice the soft, smooth saxophone and the relaxed groove, and the warm, easy voice of Withers singing over it without effort.

artiest/bill-wyman.text:
Bill Wyman is an English bassist, born on 24 October 1936 as William George Perks in Lewisham in south London. He grew up in Penge in a poor family and described his wartime childhood as marked by poverty. In 1955 he joined the Royal Air Force and was stationed in Germany. There he heard the first rock 'n' roll in dance halls and on the American forces radio station. He bought a guitar and in 1957 formed a skiffle group. Later he switched to bass guitar and built a fretless bass. In 1964 he officially changed his surname to Wyman.

On 7 December 1962 he auditioned, in a pub in Chelsea, for an R&B band called The Rolling Stones. He was hired as the successor to Dick Taylor, partly thanks to his instrument and his amplifiers. He was the oldest member of the group, played on the first nineteen studio albums and in the early years often sang backing vocals. In Another Land, on the album Their Satanic Majesties Request, is his; it was also released as a single and became his first solo single. Besides the Stones he made solo records, including Monkey Grip in 1974 and Stone Alone in 1976. From 1997 to 2018 he played in Bill Wyman's Rhythm Kings. In 1993 he left the Stones.

Wyman belonged to the first stable line-up of one of the biggest rock bands. In 1989 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame with the Stones. His bass was not a solo instrument, but held the band together.
artiest/bill-wyman.listen: Listen to an early song by The Rolling Stones and focus on the bass, beneath the guitars and the vocals. Notice how that low register carries the rhythm and makes the songs solid.

artiest/billie-eilish.text:
Billie Eilish was born in 2001 in Los Angeles, the daughter of two actors who also made music. She and her older brother Finneas were home-schooled by their mother, who taught them the basics of songwriting. Billie played the ukulele at six, sang in a children's choir and wrote her first real song at eleven. She also took dance lessons, until an injury put an end to that in 2016.

In 2015 she put the song Ocean Eyes on SoundCloud together with Finneas, really for her dance teacher. Within two weeks it had been listened to hundreds of thousands of times, and that was the beginning. After the EP Don't Smile at Me (2017), her first album appeared in 2019, WHEN WE ALL FALL ASLEEP, WHERE DO WE GO?, made with Finneas as producer. The single bad guy reached number 1 in America. Happier Than Ever (2021) and HIT ME HARD AND SOFT (2024) followed, with Birds of a Feather. She won two Oscars, for No Time to Die from the James Bond film of the same name and for What Was I Made For? from Barbie.

Her music is often soft and intimate: whispered vocals, many layers of voices on top of one another, deep basses and small sounds. It sounds as if she is standing right beside you. At eighteen she won the four most important Grammys in a single evening. Billie Eilish showed that a teenager and her brother, at home and without a big hit factory, could change world pop. In this way she closes a long line of women in popular music who defined their own sound.
artiest/billie-eilish.listen: Listen to bad guy. Notice the heavy, thudding bass and the snapping fingers, and Billie Eilish's soft, almost whispered singing. Notice, too, how the song suddenly changes character at the end.

artiest/billie-holiday.text: Billie Holiday grew up in Baltimore and came to Harlem as a teenager, where she sang in clubs. She named Bessie Smith and Louis Armstrong as her great examples: from Smith she took the power of the blues, from Armstrong the free handling of the beat. The producer John Hammond heard her in 1933. From 1935 she made a series of records with the pianist Teddy Wilson and the saxophonist Lester Young. She sang behind the beat, bent melodies towards her own speaking tone and turned ordinary songs into personal stories. In 1939 she recorded Strange Fruit for the label Commodore, an indictment of the lynching of Black Americans. Her life was marked by addiction and persecution by the police; she died in 1959.
artiest/billie-holiday.listen: Notice how she sings just behind the accompaniment and yet never loses the beat.

artiest/billy-bauer.text:
Billy Bauer was an American jazz guitarist, born on 14 November 1915 in New York. As a child he played ukulele and banjo before switching to guitar. He played in the band of Jerry Wald, recorded with Carl Hoff in 1941 and in 1944 joined Woody Herman's First Herd. In 1946 he also played with Benny Goodman and Jack Teagarden. In small groups around the bassist Chubby Jackson and the trombonist Bill Harris he grew into a soloist in bebop.

From 1946 he worked with the pianist Lennie Tristano. The two found each other in style and approach, and their search for what they called intuitive music led in 1949 to recordings that appear on Crosscurrents, with Intuition and Digression. Later he formed a duo with the saxophonist Lee Konitz. Their recordings, including Duet For Saxophone and Guitar, were described as some of the most beautiful duet recordings in jazz, and the unusual pairing of saxophone and guitar gave the guitar a new role in jazz. He also played in the bands of the NBC Tonight Show and the Today Show, in the early years of television. Under his own name he made only one album, Plectrist in 1956.

In his last decades Bauer taught, among others Denny Dias of Steely Dan and Joe Satriani. In 1997 his autobiography Sideman appeared. He died on 17 June 2005 in New York. Bauer showed that the guitar in modern jazz could be an equal conversation partner.
artiest/billy-bauer.listen: Listen to Intuition from 1949, with Lennie Tristano, and notice how freely the musicians play. Try to follow the guitar and hear how it talks with the other instruments.

artiest/billy-bletcher.text:
Billy Bletcher was an American actor, born on 24 September 1894 in Lancaster, Pennsylvania, and died on 5 January 1979 in Los Angeles. He appeared in films from the 1910s and later on television, including in comedies of Our Gang and The Three Stooges. Even so, most people know him not by his face but by his voice: a deep, powerful, booming baritone.

In the golden age of American animation he voiced a great many cartoon characters. For Walt Disney he was Pete in the Mickey Mouse films and the Big Bad Wolf in Three Little Pigs. For MGM he voiced Spike the bulldog in Tom and Jerry, and for Warner Bros. the father Bear in Chuck Jones's The Three Bears and the wolf in Little Red Riding Rabbit from 1944. In 1939 he was hired, together with Pinto Colvig, to dub the voices of the Munchkins in The Wizard of Oz. He also voiced the Gas Cloud in the training film Gas for Private Snafu in 1944 and played roles in The Lone Ranger. For the dwarfs in Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs he was not allowed to audition for Disney, for fear that the public would recognise his voice from the shorts.

Bletcher is an example of a voice actor whose work often lies in musical cartoons and film musicals. He supplied the menace and the comic, booming voice on which the cartoons of that era rested.
artiest/billy-bletcher.listen: Watch a Mickey Mouse short from the 1930s in which Pete appears and listen to his voice. Notice how deep and broad it sounds, and what that does for the menace of the character.

artiest/billy-bragg.text:
Billy Bragg is an English singer, songwriter and political activist, born Stephen William Bragg on 20 December 1957 in Barking, Essex. His music mixes folk, punk rock and protest song, with lyrics that are mostly about politics or about love. At twelve he became interested in poetry, and later he drew inspiration from Bob Dylan, Simon and Garfunkel and from punk groups such as The Jam and The Clash. A concert by The Clash and the Rock Against Racism march of 1978 shaped his left-wing political views.

In 1977 he started the band Riff Raff, which broke up in 1980. In 1981 he enlisted in the army, but after three months he bought himself out. He then performed solo in London with an electric guitar, under the name Spy vs Spy. To get his demo to the record company Charisma, he posed as a television repairman. In July 1983 his first record appeared, Life's a Riot with Spy vs Spy, followed by Brewing Up with Billy Bragg in 1984, Talking with the Taxman about Poetry in 1986 and Workers Playtime in 1988. In 1990 he released a version of The Internationale. In 1998 he made Mermaid Avenue, with new music to words by Woody Guthrie.

Bragg showed that a man with an electric guitar and a loud voice could replace an entire arrangement, and that a pop song could also be a political pamphlet. His work stands in a line of folk and protest that runs from Guthrie through Dylan and punk to him. That is why he is the quintessential singer-songwriter of the British left.
artiest/billy-bragg.listen: Listen to a song from Life's a Riot with Spy vs Spy from 1983 and notice how little there is to hear: a voice and an electric guitar. Notice how the words then come to the foreground.

artiest/billy-cobham.text: The drummer Billy Cobham was born in Panama and grew up in New York. He played with Horace Silver and on albums by Miles Davis, such as Jack Johnson. In 1971 he became the drummer of John McLaughlin's Mahavishnu Orchestra. Cobham played a large drum kit with two bass drums and many tom-toms, with enormous power and speed in odd time signatures. His first solo album Spectrum (1973), with the guitarist Tommy Bolin and the keyboard player Jan Hammer, became a model for fusion and rock drummers. The piece Stratus was later sampled a great deal. Cobham has long lived in Switzerland.
artiest/billy-cobham.listen: Follow the drums: fast, loud and yet precise in a complicated metre.

artiest/billy-corgan.text:
Billy Corgan was born in 1967 in Chicago. His parents divorced when he was small, and he had a difficult childhood with a father who was often away. That father was a guitarist and recommended Jeff Beck and Jimi Hendrix to him, but otherwise Billy taught himself to play. He listened to Black Sabbath, Queen and Cheap Trick, and later discovered the alternative rock of Bauhaus and The Cure. After a few small bands he decided to go all in on music.

In 1988 he founded The Smashing Pumpkins in Chicago with the guitarist James Iha, the bassist D'arcy Wretzky and the drummer Jimmy Chamberlin. On the debut Gish (1991) the band mixed psychedelic rock with heavy metal. The breakthrough came in 1993 with Siamese Dream, with Today, Cherub Rock and Disarm. Corgan was seen as a control freak: on that album he played almost all the guitar and bass parts himself. In 1995 the double album Mellon Collie and the Infinite Sadness followed.

Corgan wrote the songs, sang in a high, somewhat nasal voice and built walls of distorted guitars, which he alternated with soft, dreamy passages. In this way he helped make alternative rock big in the 1990s. After the band split in 2000 he started Zwan and made solo records, before reviving The Smashing Pumpkins in 2007. He also became the owner of a wrestling promotion.
artiest/billy-corgan.listen: Listen to Today by The Smashing Pumpkins. Notice the light, almost cheerful guitar motif at the start and then the hard, distorted guitars. Read the lyrics along and hear how gloomy they are compared with the music.

artiest/billy-eckstine.text:
Billy Eckstine was an American jazz and pop singer and bandleader from the swing and bebop years. He was born on 8 July 1914 in Pittsburgh and grew up partly in Washington, D.C. In 1933 he left Howard University to become a musician, after winning an amateur contest at the Howard Theatre with an imitation of Cab Calloway. In 1939 he joined the orchestra of Earl Hines in Chicago, where until 1943 he was singer and trumpeter and had jukebox hits such as Stormy Monday Blues and his own Jelly, Jelly.

In 1944 he founded his own big band. That group was regarded as the first bebop big band and became a training ground for young musicians who shaped the future of jazz: Charlie Parker, Dizzy Gillespie, Dexter Gordon, Miles Davis, Art Blakey, Fats Navarro and Sarah Vaughan. Dizzy Gillespie later wrote that no band sounded like Eckstine's. The orchestra reached the charts with A Cottage for Sale and Prisoner of Love. In 1947 Eckstine went solo, with lush orchestrations. His 1951 recording of I Apologize was given a place in the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999, and in 2019 he received a posthumous Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award.

Eckstine had a rich, almost operatic bass-baritone. The New York Times wrote that his full, sweet way of singing inspired singers such as Johnny Hartman, Joe Williams and Lou Rawls. He belongs to the singers who joined jazz and popular music, and his orchestra brought bebop to a large audience.
artiest/billy-eckstine.listen: Listen to I Apologize from 1951 and notice his voice, which sounds deep and full. Try to hear how he lets long notes ring out, like an opera singer, without the song becoming heavy.

artiest/billy-higgins.text:
Billy Higgins was an American jazz drummer, born in 1936 in Los Angeles. From 1958 he played on the first records of the saxophonist Ornette Coleman. In the late 1950s he went to New York with Coleman, the trumpeter Don Cherry and the bassist Charlie Haden. That quartet without a piano turned the jazz world upside down with free, open music, which later came to be called free jazz. On The Shape of Jazz to Come (1959) you can hear how Higgins gave the soloists all the room with a light, mobile rhythm.

He then became one of the most sought-after drummers in jazz. He was one of the regular drummers for Blue Note and played on dozens of records from the 1960s, with Lee Morgan, Dexter Gordon, Herbie Hancock, Hank Mobley, Jackie McLean and Sonny Rollins, among others. He also played with Thelonious Monk, Pat Metheny and the pianist Cedar Walton. He felt equally at home in hard bop and free jazz. In total he played on more than seven hundred recordings, including rock and funk.

Higgins was known for his supple, swinging playing and his broad smile behind the drum kit. In 1989 he founded the cultural centre The World Stage in Los Angeles, to help young jazz musicians. He also taught at the university in Los Angeles. He died in 2001.
artiest/billy-higgins.listen: Listen to Lonely Woman by the Ornette Coleman Quartet. Notice the contrast between the slow, plaintive melody of the horns and the fast, ticking rhythm that Billy Higgins plays on his cymbals.

artiest/billy-joel.text:
Billy Joel was born on 9 May 1949 in the Bronx and grew up in Hicksville on Long Island. His mother sent him to piano lessons. He left high school for music, played in bands such as The Hassles and the duo Attila and performed in piano bars. In 1971 he made his solo debut with Cold Spring Harbor.

After a popular radio appearance in Philadelphia he was signed to Columbia, where Piano Man appeared in 1973. The title song gave him his nickname. The real breakthrough came with The Stranger (1977), with Just the Way You Are, Movin' Out (Anthony's Song) and Only the Good Die Young. 52nd Street (1978) became his first number 1 album. On Glass Houses (1980) he presented himself more as a rock artist, and It's Still Rock and Roll to Me became his first number 1 single. An Innocent Man (1983) was a tribute to the rhythm and blues and doo-wop of his youth, with Uptown Girl and The Longest Time. In 1989 he scored with We Didn't Start the Fire.

Joel wrote all his albums himself and combined pop and rock with the piano tradition and a strong sense of storytelling. In 1987 he was one of the first Western artists to make a rock tour of the Soviet Union. After River of Dreams (1993) he largely stopped making pop albums; in 2001 Fantasies & Delusions appeared, with classical piano pieces of his own. In 1999 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/billy-joel.listen: Listen to Piano Man (1973). Notice the waltzing three-four time, the harmonica between the verses and how Joel, like a narrator, introduces the regulars of a bar one by one.

artiest/billy-murray.text:
Billy Murray was an American singer and voice actor, born on 25 May 1877 in Philadelphia, the son of Irish immigrants from County Kerry. He grew up in Denver, became interested in the theatre and in 1893 joined a travelling vaudeville orchestra. In 1897 he made his first recordings in San Francisco, on cylinders that have not survived. From 1903 he recorded regularly in New York and New Jersey, where the big record companies and the Tin Pan Alley music industry were based.

Murray was one of the most popular singers in the United States in the first half of the twentieth century and worked for almost every label of his time. He became known as The Denver Nightingale. In 1906 he made the first of his duets with Ada Jones, and he also sang with Aileen Stanley, Elsie Baker and quartets such as the Haydn Quartet and the American Quartet. His tenor was powerful, with clear diction and an almost spoken way of singing, which made him the favourite singer of Thomas Edison, who was hard of hearing. In comic songs he sometimes deliberately sang a little flat.

With the electric microphone in the 1920s his style disappeared. His way of singing, which he called hammering, consisted of shouting the song into an acoustic horn, and that did not suit the new, soft way of singing known as crooning. Murray had to temper his voice. Even so, he shows what popular music sounded like before the microphone existed: loud, clear and made to fill a hall and a gramophone horn.
artiest/billy-murray.listen: Find a recording by Billy Murray from the acoustic era and hear how clearly every word can be understood. Notice that he almost shouts, because he had no microphone then.

artiest/billy-preston.text:
Billy Preston was born in 1946 in Houston and grew up in Los Angeles. He was a child prodigy who taught himself to play, without ever having had lessons. At ten he was already accompanying gospel singers such as Mahalia Jackson on the organ, and at eleven he sang on television with Nat King Cole. In 1962 he became the organist in Little Richard's band. During a performance in Hamburg he got to know The Beatles there. Later he played with Sam Cooke and Ray Charles.

In January 1969 George Harrison brought him in during the tense recording sessions for Get Back. Preston played organ and electric piano and also stood on the roof at the band's last performance. The single Get Back was released as The Beatles with Billy Preston, the only time the group credited another musician in this way. For that reason he is called one of the fifth Beatles. On the Apple label he made That's the Way God Planned It (1969) with Harrison.

In the 1970s he scored hits of his own such as Outa-Space, with which he made the sound of the clavinet popular in funk, Will It Go Round in Circles and Nothing from Nothing. He co-wrote You Are So Beautiful for Joe Cocker and for years played keyboards with The Rolling Stones. Preston brought gospel, soul, funk and rock together in his playing. In 2021 he was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
artiest/billy-preston.listen: Listen to Get Back by The Beatles with Billy Preston. Notice Preston's electric piano, which plays along throughout the song and halfway through gets a swinging solo of its own.

artiest/billy-ray-cyrus.text:
Billy Ray Cyrus was born in 1961 in Flatwoods, Kentucky. His grandfather was a minister in a Pentecostal congregation, and Billy Ray grew up amid bluegrass and gospel. He went to college on a baseball scholarship, but after a Neil Diamond concert he decided to become a musician. In the 1980s he played in the band Sly Dog. It was a hard time: in Los Angeles he slept for a period in his neighbours' car. In 1990 he signed with Mercury.

His debut album Some Gave All appeared in 1992 and was an enormous success. It spent seventeen weeks in a row at number 1 on the American album chart, longer than any debut by a country artist. The big hit was Achy Breaky Heart, a cheerful, simple country song that also caught on outside America. Thanks to the video, line dancing became a craze all over the world. He went on making albums and became an actor, including in the Disney series Hannah Montana, alongside his daughter Miley Cyrus.

In 2019 he was in the news again. Lil Nas X had made a song, Old Town Road, that mixed country and hip hop, and a discussion arose about whether it was country at all. Cyrus sang on a remix, and that version spent nineteen weeks at number 1 in America. It earned him his first two Grammys. In this way a country star of the 1990s became a bridge between country and the hip hop of the streaming age.
artiest/billy-ray-cyrus.listen: Listen to the remix of Old Town Road by Lil Nas X with Billy Ray Cyrus. Notice the banjo and the hip hop beat with deep basses, and hear how Cyrus's voice gives the song a real country side.

artiest/billy-squier.text:
Billy Squier was born in 1950 in Wellesley, Massachusetts. As a child he took piano lessons, but a second-hand guitar from a classmate brought him to rock. At fourteen he had his first little band. In 1968 he saw Eric Clapton play with Cream in a Boston club, and from then on he took music seriously. In the mid-1970s he was singer and writer of the band Piper, which supported Kiss.

In 1980 his first solo album appeared, The Tale of the Tape. It included The Big Beat, which did not become a hit at the time. His breakthrough came with Don't Say No (1981), produced by Reinhold Mack, who also worked with Queen. Hits such as The Stroke, In the Dark and My Kinda Lover, and the radio favourite Lonely Is the Night, made him a star of arena rock: solid guitar riffs, powerful drums and choruses to sing along to. Emotions in Motion (1982) and Signs of Life (1984) were also successful. After that his popularity fell quickly, according to many because of an unfortunate video.

His lasting influence came from an unexpected direction. The drum break at the start of The Big Beat became one of the most sampled drum parts ever. Run-DMC, Jay-Z, Alicia Keys and Dizzee Rascal used it. In this way the work of a white rock singer of the 1980s lives on in hip hop.
artiest/billy-squier.listen: Listen to the start of The Big Beat. Notice the heavy, reverberating drums that play alone for a few bars. Then try to hear the same rhythm again in Girl on Fire by Alicia Keys.

artiest/billy-strayhorn.text: Billy Strayhorn grew up in Pittsburgh and as a teenager had already written the song Lush Life. In 1938 he showed his work to Duke Ellington, who took him on. For almost thirty years he worked as composer, arranger and second pianist of the orchestra. He wrote Take the 'A' Train, which from 1941 became the band's signature tune, and ballads such as Chelsea Bridge. Often it is no longer possible to tell which part of a piece by Ellington is Ellington's and which is Strayhorn's. Strayhorn lived openly as a gay man, which was rare at the time, and committed himself to the civil rights movement. He died in 1967 of cancer.
artiest/billy-strayhorn.listen: Hear the rich chords beneath the melody: more refined than ordinary dance music.

artiest/bing-crosby.text:
Bing Crosby was an American singer and actor, one of the first stars to be big on record, radio and film at the same time. He was born in 1903 in Tacoma, in the state of Washington, and grew up in Spokane. At home the phonograph was often on loud and his mother sang. As a boy he preferred to whistle and hum rather than sing. His nickname Bing came from a comic strip in the local newspaper. In 1923 he became the drummer in a band of schoolboys, and afterwards he performed in theatres.

Crosby's career began at the time when microphones and recording technology were improving. As a result he no longer had to shout to be heard above an orchestra. He sang softly and relaxed, close to the microphone, as if he were addressing the listener personally. That intimate way of singing, called crooning, became a model for Frank Sinatra, Perry Como and later also Elvis Presley and John Lennon. He recorded more than 1,600 songs and appeared in over seventy films. In the film Holiday Inn (1942) he sang White Christmas by Irving Berlin. Ever since, his voice has belonged to Christmas.

Crosby also changed the music industry. After seeing a German tape recorder he invested in the company Ampex, and he was the first to pre-record his radio shows on magnetic tape. In this way recordings could be cut and redone, which became the standard. During the Second World War he was seen as the man who did the most for the morale of the soldiers. He died in 1977.
artiest/bing-crosby.listen: Listen to White Christmas. Notice the form of the song: can you hear where the first part keeps returning and where the bridge, the middle section with a different melody, begins? Notice, too, how calmly and closely Crosby sings.

artiest/binker-and-moses.text:
Binker and Moses is a British jazz duo of the saxophonist Binker Golding and the drummer Moses Boyd, formed in London in 2014. Boyd, born on 30 April 1991 in Catford in south London, learned to drum at school and studied jazz drums at the Trinity Laban Conservatoire. He took part in the education programme Tomorrow's Warriors, to which the London jazz scene of recent years owes a great deal. The duo made four albums: Dem Ones in 2015, Journey to the Mountain of Forever in 2017, Alive in the East? in 2018 and Feeding the Machine in 2022. With them it won, among other things, a MOBO Award, two Jazz FM Awards and a Parliamentary Jazz Award.

Boyd also works under his own name. His debut album Dark Matter from 2020 was nominated for the Mercury Prize, and he leads the group Moses Boyd Exodus, in which Golding also plays. His music mixes jazz with grime, electronics, highlife and broken beat, and he sees it as a continuation of Black music and the diaspora, with influences from afrobeats, soca, reggae, drum and bass and jungle. He names Kind of Blue by Miles Davis and Boy in Da Corner by Dizzee Rascal as major influences.

Boyd is one of the faces of the London jazz world. The Guardian called him a founding figure of the current London jazz scene. The duo shows that a saxophone and a drum kit are enough for a full, danceable sound, and that jazz can belong in club culture.
artiest/binker-and-moses.listen: Listen to a piece from Alive in the East? from 2018 and notice how the saxophone and the drums follow each other. Try to hear who is leading and who is holding the rhythm for the other.

artiest/bireli-lagrene.text:
Biréli Lagrène is a French jazz guitarist, born on 4 September 1966 in Soufflenheim in Alsace. He comes from a Sinti family and grew up in the tradition of Gypsy guitar: his father and grandfather were guitarists. He began playing at four or five and at seven was already improvising jazz in the style of Django Reinhardt, whom his father admired and whom he wanted his sons to follow. In 1980, as a teenager, he recorded his first album, Routes to Django: Live at the Krokodil, which was released in 1981 on Jazzpoint.

In the years that followed he toured with guitarists such as Al Di Meola, Paco de Lucía and John McLaughlin, and played with Benny Carter, Benny Goodman and Stéphane Grappelli. In 1984 he performed in New York with Larry Coryell and Vic Juris, at a tribute to Reinhardt. Later he also worked with Jaco Pastorius, Stanley Clarke, the Gil Evans Orchestra and Charlie Haden, and in 1989 in a duo with Stanley Jordan. His albums range from Inferno in 1987 and Foreign Affairs in 1988 to Standards in 1992 and My Favorite Django in 1995. He plays swing, jazz fusion and post-bop, and according to the Dutch Wikipedia also masters bass, violin and piano.

Lagrène received, among other honours, three Django d'Or awards, in 1993, 2002 and 2007, and in 2012 the French distinction Chevalier des Arts et des Lettres. He keeps the Sinti swing of Django Reinhardt alive, but with his fast, clear playing also moves towards fusion and other styles.
artiest/bireli-lagrene.listen: Listen to a recording of My Favorite Django from 1995 and notice the speed of his guitar. Hear how he plays many notes in a short time and yet lets a melody come through.
